newsitem.title: FRANCE: French govt spells out deficit-cutting aims - paper.
newsitem.headline: French govt spells out deficit-cutting aims - paper.

text.p: The French government aims to cut the budget deficit by 92.9 billion francs in five years, according to its five-year budget plan submitted on Tuesday to the National Assembly, the newspaper Le Monde said.

According to the plan, which the newspaper said was more of a "moral commitment than a formal pledge", the government would cut the budget deficit from 283.70 billion francs in 1997 to 257.3 billion in 1998, to 236.9 billion in 1999, 214.80 billion in 2000 and 190.8 billion in 2001.
Each year, the fall in the deficit would amount to between 20.4 billion and 26.4 billion francs.

As a result, the budget deficit should fall to 3.45 percent of GDP in 1997 to two percent in 2001 under national accounting criteria and from 2.9 percent to 1.9 percent according to European Union criteria.

The deficit-cutting will mean tight control of spending. Over the next five years, spending should not increase more than 71 billion francs, going from 1,552.9 billion francs in 1997 to 1,624 billion francs in 2001, the newspaper said.
"When growth is more dynamic, the government will utilise its margin for manoeuvre to accelerate deficit reduction...at the same time as easing taxes," the newspaper quoted the report.
"The tax reduction will be carried out first through the suppression of exceptional increases in TVA (value added tax) and on taxes on companies imposed in 1995.

It said the government was basing its forecast on expectations of around 2.5 percent growth a year. The government has forecast growth of 2.3 percent for 1997 and has predicted growth of 2.5 percent in 1998.
Finance Minister Jean Arthuis announced last month that he planned to reduce the total public deficit to below two percent in 2001 from a forecast three percent next year.
Earlier five-year plans by this and the previous government have failed to meet their objectives.
